title: Empathy

learn.summary: Empathy is feeling with someone; it has cognitive (understanding their state), affective (feeling it), and motivational (caring about it) components. Compassion researchers like Tania Singer distinguish empathy from compassion: empathy alone can burn you out through shared distress, while compassion adds warmth and the wish to help — and shows different brain signatures. The goal is not maximal feeling but accurate understanding plus care.

do: After your next disagreement, write two sentences stating the other person's position so fairly they would sign off on it.

children.title: Empathy vs Sympathy

learn.summary: Sympathy observes from the outside ('poor you'); empathy climbs in ('I am with you'). Brené Brown popularized the distinction: sympathy often starts with 'at least...' and creates distance, while empathy requires taking the other's perspective and staying out of judgment. Rarely does an empathic response begin with 'at least.'

do: Catch yourself once this week starting a response with 'at least' or 'well, on the bright side' — and swap it for 'that sounds really hard.'

children.title: Perspective-Taking

learn.summary: Actively imagining another's viewpoint reduces stereotyping and increases helping — but imagining their situation ('what would it be like to be them') works better than projecting yourself into it ('what would I do'). The fundamental attribution error is the enemy here: we explain our own failures by circumstances and others' failures by character. Perspective-taking is the deliberate correction.

do: Next time someone cuts you off or snaps at you, generate three situational explanations (running late, bad news, in pain) before settling on a character judgment.

children.title: Empathic Accuracy Limits

learn.summary: William Ickes's research on empathic accuracy found people correctly infer a partner's thoughts and feelings only around 20–35% of the time — even spouses. The humbling implication: your gut read of someone is a hypothesis, not a fact. The fix is not more intuition but more checking: 'I am guessing you are frustrated — is that right?'

do: Twice this week, state your read of someone's feeling as a question ('you seem stressed — am I off?') and track how often you were wrong.

children.title: Empathy Blockers

learn.summary: Rosenberg cataloged the habits that kill empathy mid-sentence: advising, one-upping, educating, consoling, story-telling, shutting down, sympathizing, interrogating, explaining, and correcting. All are well-intentioned; all move the spotlight off the speaker. Knowing your personal favorite blocker is half the battle — most people have one they reach for automatically.

do: Identify your default blocker (advising? one-upping? silver-lining?) and tally each time you catch it over the next three days.

reflect: Whose situation did you dismiss quickly this week? Sit with what their day might actually feel like from the inside.
